Refrigerant cycle — log p–h (EOS vapour · liquid approx.)
Cycle on a log p–h chart with the compression state from real superheated-vapour properties (CoolProp HEOS, IIR reference): evaporation at 3.0°C, condensing at 46.3°C, 12.0K superheat, 11.3K subcooling. Discharge state 2 is computed at the condenser pressure from the isentropic state and the efficiency below. The vapour and compression states are HEOS-backed; the subcooled-liquid state 3 is approximated from the saturation curve (not a full pressure–temperature liquid state), which can add a few percent to COP at high condensing temperature with large subcooling.

Psychrometric Chart (T–W)
Entering and leaving air plotted on a live psychrometric chart at 101.5 kPa. The red line is the cooling process; its slope shows the sensible/latent split. Saturation, RH and enthalpy grid use the same psychrometric formulas (Buck saturation, humidity ratio, enthalpy) as the capacity result, evaluated at the actual barometric pressure. The chart re-implements those formulas rather than sharing one stored state, so they agree by construction but are not a single code path.
Entering air (Inn)
1

Dry-Bulb (DB)

PT100 or NTC probe, duct center, 30-50 cm from bends. Wait 3-5 min. Take 3 readings and average. Never use IR gun.

2

Relative Humidity (RH)

Calibrated capacitive hygrometer. Return air 40-60% RH. Wait 3-5 min. Cross-check with sling psychrometer if possible.

Leaving air (Ut)
3

Dry-Bulb (DB)

10-20 cm from outlet, center of airstream. Avoid condensate zone below coil. PT100 only. Wait min 5 min.

4

Relative Humidity (RH)

Supply air is 85-95% RH - hardest to measure. Allow 5-10 min stabilisation. Avoid water droplets on sensor. Best: measure WB with sling psychrometer and convert.

Airflow — three methods, best first
5a

Best — duct traverse (if a straight duct exists)

If the unit connects to ductwork with a straight run (≥7.5 duct-diameters upstream, ≥3 downstream of any bend or damper), use the multi-point traverse panel below. It applies the log-Tchebycheff / equal-area rule and is the most accurate field method. Prefer this whenever a duct is accessible.

5b

Field standard — capture hood / funnel (no duct)

On a free-blowing indoor unit (split, cassette, console) there is no duct to traverse and a sensor held in front of the grille reads a turbulent mix of supply and room air — easily 20–30% wrong. Build a funnel/hood that captures ALL the air and channels it through a known cross-section where one clean velocity reading represents the whole flow. Sizing is below. Measured against the liquid side or a balometer, a well-built hood lands within a few percent.

5c

Last resort — free sensor reading (no duct, no hood)

If neither is possible, grid at least 5 points evenly across the grille face, average them, and multiply by the grille free-area factor (0.65–0.80 depending on louvre blockage). Treat the result as ±15–25%: enter that figure in the GUM uncertainty panel so the capacity confidence reflects it. Do not present this as a verified airflow.

Power
6

Compressor power (kW)

Clamp meter on live wire. Record kW not kVA. Steady-state only. Inverter units: average over 1 min.

Building a capture hood / funnel (method 5b)

Goal: catch every bit of the unit's air and force it through ONE throat of known area, then read a single clean velocity there. Flow (m³/h) = throat velocity (m/s) × throat area (m²) × 3600 — or feed that velocity straight into the traverse panel as a 1-point round duct of the throat diameter.

Shape & throat size by machine
Throat sized so velocity lands in the meter's sweet spot (2–10 m/s):
· Small split / console (≲3.5 kW, ~300–700 m³/h): throat 150–200 mm Ø or 150×150 mm
· Mid split / cassette (3.5–7 kW, ~700–1300 m³/h): throat 200–250 mm Ø
· Large cassette / ducted (7–14 kW, ~1300–2500 m³/h): throat 300–350 mm Ø, or split into two throats
Rule of thumb: throat area ≈ peak flow (m³/s) ÷ 6 m/s.
Geometry that keeps it accurate
· Mouth must seal over the WHOLE grille (foam/brush gasket) — any leak is lost flow
· Taper gently: cone half-angle ≤ 15–20° so flow doesn't separate from the walls
· After the taper add a straight throat ≥ 3 throat-diameters long before the sensor
· Put the sensor centred, ~2 throat-diameters into the straight part, perpendicular to flow
· A few drinking-straws / honeycomb at throat entry straightens swirl from cassettes

Materials: appliance cardboard or corrugated plastic (Coroplast), aluminium tape, foam weatherstrip for the seal. Modular tip: build several mouth adapters (one per common grille size) that all neck down to ONE standard throat tube, so you keep a single calibrated throat. Sanity check: for a cooling unit you can cross-check hood airflow against the liquid-side or psychrometric capacity — if they disagree by >10%, suspect a hood leak or a separated cone.

Enthalpy accuracy: A 2% RH error at 90% supply RH causes approx 1.5 kJ/kg enthalpy error. With 0.2 kg/s airflow this is 0.3 kW error in Q - roughly 5-10% on a residential unit. Always allow full stabilisation and cross-check RH with wet-bulb measurement where precision matters.
